subsystems.name: Cell source
subsystems.role: supplies the muscle, fat and connective-tissue cells that will grow into meat.
parts: stem cells or muscle satellite cells
stable cell lines that divide indefinitely in culture

subsystems.name: Culture medium
subsystems.role: the liquid food the cells live in — sugars, amino acids, vitamins, salts and signalling proteins.

subsystems.name: Scaffold material
subsystems.role: an edible, food-grade matrix that cells can attach to and pull on, so they organise into fibres instead of a shapeless slurry.
parts: hydrogels such as alginate, gelatin or collagen
plant proteins such as soy, pea or zein
polysaccharides such as cellulose or chitosan

subsystems.name: Scaffold fabrication
subsystems.role: shapes the matrix into the geometry of a cut of meat, with pores and channels for nutrients.
parts: decellularised plant tissue as a ready-made vascular template

subsystems.name: Bioreactor and perfusion
subsystems.role: keeps cells fed with oxygen and nutrients and removes waste as the tissue thickens.
parts: agitated suspension tanks for cell expansion
perfusion chambers that push medium through the scaffold
microcarriers or edible beads for anchorage-dependent cells

subsystems.name: Maturation and downstream processing
subsystems.role: turns a grown construct into something that cooks and chews like meat.
parts: mechanical or electrical stimulation to align muscle fibres

buildSteps.title: Take a biopsy
buildSteps.detail: A small sample of muscle or fat is taken from a live animal under anaesthesia; the animal stays healthy and the sample is the only animal input needed.

buildSteps.title: Establish a cell line
buildSteps.detail: Cells are selected and adapted so they can divide many times in a stirred tank without turning into the wrong cell type. Creating an immortal, stable line is the hardest biological step.

buildSteps.title: Expand the cells
buildSteps.detail: The cells are grown in progressively larger bioreactors — millilitres to litres to thousands of litres — fed with a serum-free medium whose growth factors dominate the cost.

buildSteps.title: Formulate the scaffold ink
buildSteps.detail: Edible hydrogel and plant protein are blended with a crosslinking agent so the mixture can be printed, spun or frozen while staying soft enough for cells to move through.

buildSteps.title: Make the scaffold
buildSteps.detail: The material is printed or electrospun into a fibre-like architecture, or a plant leaf or fruit is decellularised to leave its natural capillary network behind, leaving pores roughly 100–500 µm wide so cells can migrate and medium can flow.

buildSteps.title: Seed and grow
buildSteps.detail: Cells are mixed into or layered onto the scaffold. Because oxygen only diffuses about 100–200 µm into living tissue, constructs thicker than a fraction of a millimetre must be perfused with medium through internal channels.

buildSteps.title: Mature the tissue
buildSteps.detail: Weeks of perfusion, gentle mechanical stretching and feeding align the muscle cells into fibres and let fat cells accumulate, which is what produces texture and flavour.

buildSteps.title: Harvest and assemble
buildSteps.detail: The grown tissue is washed free of medium, combined with cultivated fat, and portioned into a product that can be cooked like conventional meat.

buildSteps.title: Clear regulation
buildSteps.detail: Before sale, a novel-food safety assessment is required; a handful of countries have completed this only for thin, unstructured chicken products.

prerequisites.why: serum-free formulations exist, but growth factors and purification make them far too expensive to compete with farmed meat.
alginate, collagen, cellulose and plant proteins are already approved food ingredients; the gap is shaping them into stable 3D structures.
medical bioreactors operate at millilitre to litre scale; meat needs cubic metres with cheap, single-use components.
cells that divide indefinitely and still behave like muscle or fat are the difference between laboratory batches and a factory.
only a few jurisdictions have approved cultivated meat, and only for untextured products.

pathway.milestone: small volumes of cultivated chicken on sale in a handful of markets
pathway.unlocks: real regulatory and consumer experience, though at high cost.

pathway.milestone: hybrid products blending plant protein with cultivated fat or a few percent cultivated cells
pathway.unlocks: cost reduction and shelf presence while full scaffolds mature.

pathway.milestone: perfused, edible scaffolds producing whole-cut textures at pilot scale
pathway.unlocks: steaks, fillets and other structured products rather than minced or shredded formats.

pathway.milestone: reusable cell lines, animal-component-free medium and cubic-metre perfusion lines running continuously
pathway.unlocks: production costs approaching those of conventional meat and genuine food-security volumes.
